Reserved concurrency on the function
A larger function timeout
explanation: Provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of execution environments initialised and warm, which eliminates cold starts for those invocations.
distractors: Queuing adds latency and changes the API to asynchronous, which does not suit a latency-sensitive synchronous API.
Reserved concurrency caps how much of the account concurrency pool the function may use; it does not keep environments warm.
Timeouts govern maximum runtime and are unrelated to initialisation latency.

stem: A database on EC2 needs sustained 60,000 IOPS with sub-millisecond latency on a single volume. Which EBS volume type should be used?
options: st1
gp2
io2 Block Express
gp3
explanation: io2 Block Express supports up to 256,000 provisioned IOPS with sub-millisecond latency and 99.999 percent durability, which is the tier intended for demanding single-volume database workloads.
distractors: st1 is a throughput-optimised HDD intended for large sequential reads, not high IOPS.
gp2 also caps at 16,000 IOPS and requires oversizing the volume to approach it.
gp3 tops out at 16,000 IOPS per volume, below the requirement.

stem: An application uploads very large files to S3 from offices worldwide, and uploads are slow. Which feature should be enabled?
options: S3 Select
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Transfer Acceleration
Cross-Region Replication
explanation: Transfer Acceleration routes uploads to the nearest CloudFront edge location and then over the optimised AWS backbone to the bucket, which markedly improves long-distance upload throughput.
distractors: S3 Select retrieves a subset of an object's contents; it does not affect uploads.
Intelligent-Tiering is a cost feature that moves objects between access tiers.
Replication copies objects after they arrive and does nothing for upload speed.

stem: A tightly coupled HPC workload requires the lowest possible network latency and highest bandwidth between nodes. What should be configured?
options: A spread placement group across three Availability Zones
A partition placement group
An Auto Scaling group with cross-zone load balancing
A cluster placement group in a single Availability Zone
explanation: A cluster placement group packs instances into the same high-bisection-bandwidth network segment in one AZ, which delivers the lowest inter-node latency. Combine with an Elastic Fabric Adapter for HPC traffic.
distractors: A spread group deliberately separates instances onto distinct hardware, which increases latency between them.
Partition groups isolate racks for large distributed systems; they do not minimise latency.
Load balancing distributes client traffic and is unrelated to node-to-node latency.

stem: A read-heavy application's relational database is CPU-bound serving the same catalogue queries thousands of times per second. What is the most effective change?
options: Increase the database instance size
Add an ElastiCache for Redis cache in front of the database using a cache-aside strategy
Enable Multi-AZ on the database
Convert the database to DynamoDB
explanation: Repeated identical reads are the textbook case for a cache. Serving them from Redis removes the load from the database entirely, at a fraction of the cost of scaling the database.
distractors: Vertical scaling is expensive and only postpones the problem while the query pattern remains identical.
Multi-AZ improves availability; the standby serves no reads.
A wholesale migration to DynamoDB is a large change and may not suit the relational query patterns.

stem: A containerised application must run without the team managing any EC2 instances, and the team does not want to operate Kubernetes. Which combination should be chosen?
options: Amazon EKS with managed node groups
Amazon EC2 with Docker installed via user data
Amazon ECS with the EC2 launch type
Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type
explanation: Fargate is serverless compute for containers, so there are no instances to patch, scale or secure, and ECS avoids the operational surface of Kubernetes.
distractors: EKS introduces Kubernetes, which the team explicitly does not want, and managed node groups still involve EC2 instances.
Running Docker on raw EC2 is the highest operational overhead of the options.
The EC2 launch type means you own and manage the container instances.

stem: Scale-out events take eight minutes because user data installs a long chain of dependencies at boot. What is the best fix?
options: Switch to a larger instance type
Increase the Auto Scaling group's maximum capacity
Build a golden AMI containing the dependencies, using EC2 Image Builder
Enable detailed monitoring for faster alarms
explanation: Pre-baking dependencies into an AMI removes almost all boot-time work, cutting launch time to well under a minute. Image Builder automates building, patching and testing that AMI.
distractors: A bigger instance may install marginally faster but the fundamental work is still done at boot.
A higher maximum permits more instances but does not make them boot faster.
Faster alarms shorten detection, not instance start-up time.

stem: A machine-learning training cluster needs a POSIX file system delivering hundreds of GB/s over a dataset that already lives in Amazon S3. Which service should be used?
options: Amazon EFS with Max I/O performance mode
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon EBS io2 volumes attached to each node
Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket
explanation: FSx for Lustre is a parallel file system built for HPC and machine learning, scaling to hundreds of GB/s, and it can present an S3 bucket as its file system and write results back.
distractors: EFS Max I/O raises throughput but not to Lustre's level, and it does not integrate with S3 as a data repository.
FSx for Windows serves SMB workloads and is not an HPC file system.
EBS volumes are per-instance block storage, not a shared parallel file system.

stem: An application performs 12,000 GET requests per second against a single S3 prefix and experiences 503 slow-down errors. What should be changed?
options: Distribute the objects across multiple prefixes so requests are spread over more partitions
Enable requester pays on the bucket
Enable S3 versioning
Move the bucket to S3 Standard-IA
explanation: S3 supports at least 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix. Spreading keys across more prefixes multiplies the available request rate, and the client can parallelise across them.
distractors: Requester pays shifts billing to the caller and has no performance effect.
Versioning adds object versions and does not affect throughput limits.
Standard-IA reduces storage cost and adds retrieval fees; it does not raise the request rate.

stem: An API Gateway REST API is being overwhelmed by traffic spikes that the backend cannot absorb, and responses are timing out. Requests must not be lost. What should be implemented?
options: Enable API Gateway throttling to return 429 responses
Increase the Lambda function memory allocation
Enable API Gateway caching on the stage
Put the requests into an SQS queue and process them asynchronously
explanation: Buffering with SQS decouples the arrival rate from the processing rate, so every request is durably captured and processed as capacity allows. Throttling protects the backend but rejects requests, which the requirement forbids.
distractors: Throttling returns 429 and drops the excess, which loses requests.
More memory speeds each invocation but does not prevent overload or loss.
Caching only helps for repeated identical reads and does nothing for write traffic.

stem: A company has 30 VPCs across 5 accounts that must all reach a shared services VPC and an on-premises data centre. Which design has the least ongoing management overhead?
options: VPC peering between every pair of VPCs
PrivateLink endpoints between every pair of VPCs
A separate Site-to-Site VPN from each VPC to the data centre
A Transit Gateway shared via AWS RAM, with all VPCs and the VPN or Direct Connect attached to it
explanation: Transit Gateway is a hub that each VPC attaches to once, supports transitive routing, and can be shared across accounts with RAM. Its route tables also allow segmentation, so spokes can reach shared services without reaching each other.
distractors: A full mesh of 30 VPCs needs 435 peering connections, is not transitive, and every route table must be maintained by hand.
PrivateLink exposes individual services, not general VPC-to-VPC routing, and would need an endpoint per service per consumer.
Thirty separate VPN connections multiply cost and management, and still do not connect the VPCs to each other.

stem: A company needs a petabyte-scale data warehouse for complex analytical joins across years of historical data, with high concurrency for BI users. Which service is appropriate?
options: Amazon Redshift
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon Athena
explanation: Redshift is a columnar MPP data warehouse designed for petabyte-scale OLAP workloads with complex joins and many concurrent BI users, and Redshift Spectrum can additionally query data left in S3.
distractors: RDS is an OLTP engine and does not scale to petabyte analytical workloads.
DynamoDB is a key-value store and does not perform analytical joins.
Athena is excellent for ad-hoc queries but is not designed for sustained high-concurrency BI workloads at this scale.

stem: A team needs to search across millions of application log entries by free text and visualise trends on dashboards. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon Redshift
Amazon QuickSight alone
Amazon Athena
explanation: OpenSearch Service provides full-text indexing with relevance ranking and includes OpenSearch Dashboards for visualisation, which is the standard log analytics stack on AWS.
distractors: Redshift is a SQL warehouse, not a search engine.
QuickSight visualises data from a source; it is not itself a search or storage engine.
Athena runs SQL over S3 and has no full-text relevance search or built-in dashboards.

stem: Which Route 53 routing policy should be used when European users must be served exclusively from a European Region for regulatory reasons?
options: Geoproximity routing with a bias
Latency-based routing
Weighted routing
Geolocation routing
explanation: Geolocation routing selects the answer based on the user's country or continent, which is the correct control when the requirement is legal or regulatory rather than performance.
distractors: Geoproximity shifts traffic by distance and bias but is not an exact jurisdiction control.
Latency routing optimises speed and could legitimately send a European user to a non-European Region, breaking the requirement.
Weighted routing splits traffic by ratio regardless of user location.

stem: A workload can be recompiled for ARM and the team wants better price-performance without reducing capacity. What should be changed?
options: Move to burstable t-family instances
Move to AWS Graviton-based instance types
Enable enhanced networking
Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the current types
explanation: Graviton processors typically deliver around 20 percent better price-performance than comparable x86 instances for workloads that can run on ARM, with no loss of capacity.
distractors: Burstable instances trade sustained performance for a low baseline, which risks reducing capacity under load.
Enhanced networking improves packet throughput but does not change price-performance for a compute-bound workload.
Reserved Instances reduce price but do not improve performance and lock in the current architecture.

stem: An application must run a job every night at 02:00 UTC with the least operational overhead. What should be used?
options: An Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule targeting the job
A Step Functions Wait state in an infinite loop
An SQS delay queue with a 24-hour delay
A cron entry on a dedicated EC2 instance
explanation: EventBridge Scheduler runs cron and rate expressions at scale with retries and no infrastructure, invoking Lambda, ECS, Step Functions and many other targets.
distractors: An infinite Wait loop is fragile, costly and abuses the service.
SQS delay queues are capped at 15 minutes, so a 24-hour delay is not possible.
A dedicated instance must be patched, monitored and made highly available, which is significant overhead for a nightly job.

stem: A company must migrate an on-premises Oracle database to Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal downtime. Which combination should be used? (Choose TWO.)
options: AWS Schema Conversion Tool to convert the schema and stored procedures
Amazon RDS Multi-AZ to replicate from Oracle
AWS DataSync to copy the database files
AWS Snowball Edge to ship the database files
AWS Database Migration Service with ongoing change data capture replication
explanation: SCT converts schema objects when the engine changes; DMS then performs a full load followed by continuous replication of ongoing changes, so cutover happens with only seconds of downtime.
distractors: Multi-AZ is an availability feature within RDS and cannot replicate from an on-premises Oracle database.
DataSync copies files, not live database state, and would require extended downtime.
Snowball is for bulk data transfer where bandwidth is limiting; it does not provide minimal-downtime cutover.

stem: A Windows application requires a shared file system accessible over SMB with Active Directory integration. Which service should be used?
options: Amazon EFS
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon S3 File Gateway
Amazon FSx for Lustre
explanation: FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed native Windows file system supporting SMB, NTFS ACLs, DFS namespaces and Active Directory integration.
distractors: EFS uses NFS and targets Linux workloads; it does not offer native SMB with Windows ACLs.
File Gateway presents an on-premises share backed by S3 and is a hybrid appliance rather than a native cloud SMB file system.
FSx for Lustre is a POSIX HPC file system, not an SMB share.

stem: A nightly video encoding job is fully checkpointed and can be restarted at any time. Which purchasing option minimises cost?
options: Dedicated Hosts
On-Demand Instances
Standard Reserved Instances for one year
Spot Instances requested through an EC2 Fleet with the capacity-optimized strategy
explanation: Interruptible, fault-tolerant, time-flexible workloads are the textbook Spot case, saving up to 90 percent. Requesting across several instance types with the capacity-optimized strategy minimises interruptions.
distractors: Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive option and are used for socket-bound licensing requirements.
On-Demand carries no discount at all.
Reserved Instances suit steady always-on usage, not a job that runs for part of each night.

stem: A company runs a steady 24/7 EC2 fleet and plans to move some services to AWS Fargate and Lambda within the year. Which commitment gives the best discount without stranding the investment?
options: Standard Reserved Instances
An EC2 Instance Savings Plan
Convertible Reserved Instances
A Compute Savings Plan
explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply across any instance family, size, Region and operating system, and additionally cover Fargate and Lambda, so the commitment keeps applying after the migration.
distractors: Standard RIs are tied to a specific configuration and cover EC2 only.
EC2 Instance Savings Plans lock the commitment to one instance family in one Region and do not cover Fargate or Lambda.
Convertible RIs allow exchanges within EC2 but still do not cover Fargate or Lambda.

stem: An enterprise has Oracle licences that are counted per physical CPU socket and must be brought to AWS. What should the workload run on?
options: EC2 Dedicated Hosts
Default shared tenancy EC2 instances
EC2 Dedicated Instances
Amazon RDS for Oracle in a shared tenancy
explanation: Dedicated Hosts give visibility of the physical server's sockets and cores and let you control instance placement, which is what socket-based bring-your-own-licence models require.
distractors: Shared tenancy provides no physical hardware visibility at all.
Dedicated Instances run on isolated hardware but do not expose sockets and cores or allow placement control.
RDS does not expose the underlying host, so socket-based licensing cannot be satisfied.

stem: Compliance requires records to be kept for ten years, with retrieval within 12 hours being acceptable. Which storage option is cheapest?
options: S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Standard-IA
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
explanation: Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage on AWS, with standard retrieval in about 12 hours and a 180-day minimum storage duration, which suits a ten-year retention requirement precisely.
distractors: One Zone-IA is cheaper than Standard-IA but still far more expensive than Deep Archive, and stores a single copy zone.
Standard-IA is far more expensive for decade-long retention.
Flexible Retrieval costs more and its faster retrieval times are not required here.

stem: A lifecycle rule transitions log objects to S3 Standard-IA after 3 days, but the bill has increased. Why?
options: Objects in Standard-IA cannot be deleted
Lifecycle transitions are billed per object per day
Standard-IA costs more per GB than S3 Standard
Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum billable storage duration, so objects deleted earlier are still charged for 30 days
explanation: Standard-IA charges a minimum of 30 days per object, plus a per-GB retrieval fee and a 128 KB minimum billable object size. Transitioning short-lived objects therefore costs more than leaving them in Standard.
distractors: Objects can be deleted at any time; you are simply still billed for the minimum duration.
Transitions carry a per-request charge, not a per-day charge, and it is not the main driver here.
Standard-IA has lower per-GB storage cost than Standard; the penalty is in minimums and retrieval.

stem: A new dataset has completely unpredictable access patterns and must remain instantly available. Which storage class minimises cost with the least risk?
options: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 Standard
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Standard-IA
explanation: Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent, infrequent and archive access tiers based on observed usage, with millisecond access in the instant tiers and no retrieval charges, for a small per-object monitoring fee.
distractors: Glacier Instant Retrieval carries a 90-day minimum and retrieval charges, which is risky for unknown patterns.
Standard is the safe option but does not minimise cost if much of the data goes cold.
Choosing Standard-IA on a guess risks large retrieval charges if the data turns out to be frequently accessed.

stem: A large share of the monthly bill is NAT gateway data processing charges caused by private instances reading from Amazon S3. What is the correct fix?
options: Move the instances into public subnets
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
Replace the NAT gateway with NAT instances
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and add its route to the private route tables
explanation: Gateway endpoints for S3 are free and keep the traffic entirely inside the AWS network, bypassing the NAT gateway and eliminating both the per-GB processing charge and the internet egress.
distractors: Putting private instances in public subnets exposes them and is a security anti-pattern.
Transfer Acceleration adds cost and applies to uploads from distant clients.
NAT instances shift the cost model but you then own their availability, patching and scaling, and traffic still leaves the VPC.

stem: Two hundred gp2 volumes were oversized purely to achieve the required IOPS. How can cost be reduced without losing performance?
options: Migrate them to gp3 and provision IOPS independently of volume size
Take snapshots and delete the volumes
Enable EBS fast snapshot restore
Migrate them to st1 volumes
explanation: gp3 decouples IOPS and throughput from capacity, includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s at no extra charge, and costs roughly 20 percent less per GB than gp2. The volumes can be shrunk to the size the data actually needs.
distractors: Deleting volumes removes the workload rather than optimising it.
Fast snapshot restore speeds volume creation from snapshots and adds cost.
st1 is a throughput-optimised HDD with low IOPS and cannot be a boot volume.

stem: A finance team wants to be notified by email when monthly spend is forecast to exceed a threshold. Which service should be used?
options: AWS Budgets
AWS Cost and Usage Report
AWS Pricing Calculator
AWS Cost Explorer
explanation: Budgets sets thresholds on cost or usage, alerts on both actual and forecasted breaches via SNS or email, and can trigger actions such as applying a restrictive policy.
distractors: The Cost and Usage Report delivers detailed line items to S3 for analysis, without alerting.
The Pricing Calculator estimates costs before deployment.
Cost Explorer visualises and forecasts spend but does not send threshold alerts.

stem: Management wants to know which team is responsible for each portion of the AWS bill across many accounts. What is required?
options: Enable AWS Config in all accounts
Apply cost allocation tags to resources, activate them in the billing console, and analyse in Cost Explorer
Enable detailed billing alarms in CloudWatch
Create a separate AWS account for every individual
explanation: Cost allocation tags attribute spend by team, project or environment. They must be activated in the billing console before they appear as dimensions in Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report.
distractors: Config records configuration, not cost attribution.
Billing alarms alert on total spend and do not attribute it.
Account-per-person is unmanageable; account-per-team is a valid pattern but tags are the general mechanism and work within accounts too.

stem: Development and test EC2 instances run continuously but are only used during office hours. What is the simplest way to reduce their cost?
options: Purchase three-year Standard Reserved Instances for them
Move them to a cheaper Region
Stop them outside working hours on an EventBridge schedule
Convert them to Spot Instances
explanation: Stopping instances halts compute charges (EBS storage continues). An EventBridge schedule invoking a Lambda or SSM Automation, or the AWS Instance Scheduler solution, automates this with almost no effort.
distractors: Committing for three years to instances that are idle two-thirds of the time locks in waste.
Region arbitrage gives a small percentage saving compared with simply not running them 128 hours a week.
Spot suits interruptible batch work; interactive development environments being terminated at random is disruptive.

stem: A DynamoDB table has highly predictable, steady traffic and currently uses on-demand capacity. How can cost be reduced?
options: Add a global secondary index
Switch to provisioned capacity with auto scaling
Enable point-in-time recovery
Add a DAX cluster
explanation: Provisioned capacity is considerably cheaper than on-demand for predictable traffic, and auto scaling adjusts within a min and max band to absorb variation. Reserved capacity can reduce it further.
distractors: An index adds storage and capacity cost.
PITR adds cost.
DAX adds cluster cost; it helps latency, not table pricing, and would only reduce read capacity consumption if reads are highly repetitive.

stem: A Lambda function processes files and currently runs with 512 MB of memory, taking 10 seconds per invocation. Increasing memory to 1,769 MB reduces runtime to 2 seconds. What is the likely cost effect?
options: Total cost may decrease, because Lambda bills GB-seconds and the shorter duration can more than offset the higher memory
Cost will always increase proportionally to the memory increase
Cost is unaffected because Lambda bills per invocation only
Cost will increase because more memory means more cold starts
explanation: Lambda charges per GB-second. CPU scales with allocated memory, so a function that finishes five times faster at three and a half times the memory costs less overall, as well as reducing latency.
distractors: Cost is memory multiplied by duration, so a shorter duration can more than compensate.
Lambda bills per request and per GB-second of duration.
Memory allocation does not increase cold start frequency; larger memory usually initialises faster.

stem: A company serves large volumes of static content directly from S3 to internet users and the data transfer bill is high. What reduces it most?
options: Move the bucket to S3 One Zone-IA
Enable S3 Requester Pays
Serve the content through Amazon CloudFront
Compress objects before uploading them and leave the architecture unchanged
explanation: CloudFront data transfer out is cheaper per GB than direct S3 egress, and cache hits at the edge avoid touching the origin at all, so both transfer and request costs fall.
distractors: Storage class affects storage cost, not egress rates.
Requester Pays shifts the cost to the downloader, which is only appropriate for dataset sharing, not for serving a public website.
Compression helps but the exam expects the CDN as the primary architectural answer, and it can be combined with CloudFront anyway.

stem: A development Aurora database is used for about two hours each working day and idles the rest of the time. How can cost be minimised while keeping it available on demand?
options: Take a final snapshot and delete the cluster each evening
Use Aurora Serverless v2, which scales capacity down when idle
Purchase a one-year Reserved Instance for the cluster
Enable Aurora Backtrack
explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 adjusts capacity in fine-grained increments within seconds and scales down during idle periods, so you pay close to nothing while nobody is using it.
distractors: Snapshot-and-delete works but requires daily restore operations, which is real operational overhead and delays availability.
A reservation commits to capacity that is idle most of the time.
Backtrack is a recovery feature and adds cost.

stem: Which service provides machine-learning-based right-sizing recommendations for EC2 instances, EBS volumes and Lambda functions?
options: AWS Well-Architected Tool
AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Compute Optimizer
AWS Trusted Advisor
explanation: Compute Optimizer analyses utilisation metrics and recommends optimal instance types, volume configurations and Lambda memory settings.
distractors: The Well-Architected Tool guides architectural reviews against the framework pillars.
Cost Explorer analyses spend and recommends Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, not resource sizing.
Trusted Advisor flags idle and under-utilised resources with simpler heuristics but does not provide ML-based sizing recommendations.

stem: CloudWatch Logs costs have grown steadily for years across dozens of log groups. What is the most direct fix?
options: Move the log groups to a cheaper Region
Enable CloudWatch Logs Insights
Set a retention period on the log groups and export older data to S3
Enable detailed monitoring to consolidate the logs
explanation: CloudWatch log groups retain data indefinitely by default. Setting an explicit retention period and archiving anything needed long-term to S3 (which is far cheaper per GB) stops the unbounded growth.
distractors: Log groups belong to the Region where the resources run; moving them is impractical and does not address unbounded retention.
Logs Insights is a query tool and charges per GB scanned, adding cost.
Detailed monitoring is about metric resolution and increases cost.

stem: Which of the following data transfers incurs a charge?
options: Traffic between EC2 instances in different Availability Zones of the same Region
Data uploaded from the internet into an S3 bucket
Traffic between EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone using private IP addresses
Data transferred from S3 to Amazon Athena in the same Region
explanation: Cross-Availability-Zone traffic is charged in both directions. This is a common hidden cost in multi-AZ architectures and a frequent exam target.
distractors: Inbound data transfer to AWS is free.
Traffic within an AZ over private IPv4 addresses is free.
Athena reads S3 in the same Region without a data transfer charge; you pay per TB scanned instead.

stem: An organization with 30 accounts wants volume pricing tiers to apply across all of them and unused Reserved Instance capacity to be shared. What should be configured?
options: AWS Control Tower guardrails
A separate payment method for each account
AWS Organizations with consolidated billing
AWS Budgets at the organization level
explanation: Consolidated billing aggregates usage across all member accounts so volume discount tiers are reached faster, and unused Reserved Instance and Savings Plan capacity is applied automatically across the organization.
distractors: Control Tower sets up governance guardrails and does not affect billing aggregation directly.
Separate payment methods prevent aggregation entirely.
Budgets alert on spend; they do not change pricing.

stem: A company must move 300 TB to S3. Its internet link is 500 Mbps and is already 60 percent utilised. What is the most practical approach?
options: Order several AWS Snowball Edge devices
Use S3 Transfer Acceleration with multipart uploads
Provision an AWS Direct Connect connection and transfer over it
Use AWS DataSync over the existing internet connection
explanation: About 200 Mbps of usable bandwidth moves roughly 2 TB per day, so 300 TB would take around five months. Snowball Edge devices, used in parallel, complete the migration in weeks.
distractors: Transfer Acceleration optimises the path but cannot exceed the local link capacity.
Direct Connect takes weeks to months to provision and adds recurring cost for a one-off migration.
DataSync is efficient but is still bounded by the available bandwidth, which is the constraint here.

stem: An EMR cluster runs nightly Spark jobs that tolerate node loss. How can its cost be reduced significantly?
options: Run all nodes including the master on Spot Instances
Run task nodes on Spot Instances while keeping core and master nodes On-Demand
Switch the cluster to a memory-optimised family
Enable EMR managed scaling only
explanation: Task nodes hold no HDFS data, so losing one only loses in-flight work that Spark re-schedules. Running them on Spot captures up to 90 percent savings while core and master nodes stay stable.
distractors: Losing the master node terminates the cluster, so the master should not run on Spot.
Changing family may or may not help and is unrelated to the interruption tolerance being described.
Managed scaling helps but Spot on task nodes is the far larger lever, and the two combine.

stem: Which AWS tool would you use to estimate the monthly cost of a proposed architecture before building it?
options: AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Cost and Usage Report
AWS Pricing Calculator
AWS Budgets
explanation: The Pricing Calculator models a planned architecture and produces a cost estimate that can be saved and shared, which is exactly a pre-build exercise.
distractors: Cost Explorer reports on spend that has already happened.
The Cost and Usage Report is a detailed record of incurred charges.
Budgets alerts on actual or forecast spend against thresholds for existing usage.

stem: An application encrypts 5 GB files. Why is envelope encryption used rather than calling KMS to encrypt the file directly?
options: Envelope encryption is faster because KMS uses asymmetric algorithms
Envelope encryption avoids the need for a KMS key policy
KMS cannot encrypt data stored in S3
KMS Encrypt is limited to 4 KB of data, so a locally-used data key encrypts the file while KMS protects only the data key
explanation: The KMS Encrypt API accepts up to 4 KB. GenerateDataKey returns a plaintext key and an encrypted copy; the plaintext key encrypts the payload locally and is then discarded, and the encrypted key is stored alongside the data.
distractors: The main driver is the payload size limit and local performance, not asymmetry; KMS supports symmetric keys by default.
A key policy is still required to use the key at all.
S3 integrates with KMS directly for server-side encryption; the limitation is on direct API payload size.

stem: An application's logs show the load balancer's IP address instead of the end user's. The application sits behind an Application Load Balancer. How is the client address obtained?
options: Read the X-Forwarded-For request header
Enable cross-zone load balancing
Enable proxy protocol v2 on the ALB
Switch the target group to IP target type
explanation: An ALB terminates the connection and opens a new one to the target, so the source address is the ALB. The original client address is provided in the X-Forwarded-For header.
distractors: Cross-zone load balancing changes target distribution and has no effect on source addresses.
Proxy protocol v2 is a Network Load Balancer feature, not an ALB one.
Target type affects how targets are registered, not what source IP the target observes behind an ALB.

stem: On-premises servers must access Amazon S3 privately over an existing AWS Direct Connect connection. Which options achieve this? (Choose TWO.)
options: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and add a route on-premises
Use a Direct Connect public virtual interface to reach S3 public endpoints over the private circuit
Peer the on-premises network with the VPC
Create an interface VPC endpoint for S3 and resolve it from on-premises
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
explanation: Interface endpoints are ENIs with private IP addresses that can be reached from on-premises over Direct Connect or VPN. A public VIF reaches AWS public service endpoints across the Direct Connect circuit rather than the internet.
distractors: Gateway endpoints work only via route table entries inside the VPC and cannot be reached from on-premises.
VPC peering connects VPCs; it does not connect an on-premises network.
Transfer Acceleration uses public CloudFront edge locations over the internet.

stem: A company needs to be alerted whenever the string ERROR appears more than 10 times in five minutes in an application log group. What should be configured?
options: A CloudTrail trail with an EventBridge rule
A CloudWatch Logs metric filter feeding a CloudWatch alarm on an SNS topic
Amazon Athena scheduled queries over the exported logs
AWS Config with a custom rule
explanation: A metric filter converts a log pattern into a CloudWatch metric, and an alarm on that metric with a threshold and evaluation period publishes to SNS.
distractors: CloudTrail records API activity, not application log content.
Scheduled Athena queries would work but add substantial latency, cost and operational overhead compared with a native metric filter.
Config evaluates resource configuration and cannot inspect log content.

stem: An API in front of Lambda needs the lowest cost and latency and requires only JWT authorisation and simple proxying. Which API Gateway type should be chosen?
options: REST API in a private endpoint configuration
HTTP API
WebSocket API
REST API
explanation: HTTP APIs cost roughly 70 percent less than REST APIs and have lower latency. They support JWT authorizers and Lambda proxy integration, which is all this scenario needs.
distractors: A private REST API restricts access to a VPC, which is not the stated requirement.
WebSocket APIs are for bidirectional persistent connections.
REST APIs offer API keys, usage plans, request transformation, caching and resource policies, none of which are required here, and cost more.

stem: Premium video content must be delivered globally to authenticated subscribers only, with the S3 origin remaining private, and a single authorisation covering many files.
options: S3 presigned URLs generated per object with a long expiry
CloudFront with Origin Access Control and S3 presigned URLs per file
CloudFront with Origin Access Control and signed cookies
A public S3 bucket with a bucket policy restricting referrers
explanation: Signed cookies authorise access to multiple restricted files at once after the user signs in, and OAC keeps the bucket private while CloudFront serves the content from the edge.
distractors: S3 presigned URLs bypass the CDN, giving worse global performance, and long expiries are a security risk.
Presigned URLs are per object, so a library of files means generating and managing many URLs.
Referrer checks are trivially spoofed and require a public bucket.

stem: Which caching strategy writes data to the cache at the same time as the database, guaranteeing the cache is never stale but potentially caching data that is never read?
options: Read-through with negative caching
Write-behind with a TTL
Write-through
Lazy loading (cache-aside)
explanation: Write-through updates the cache on every write, so cached data is always current, at the cost of caching items that may never be requested and adding write latency.
distractors: Read-through populates on miss like lazy loading; negative caching stores absence of a value.
Write-behind queues writes to the database asynchronously, which is a different trade-off.
Lazy loading populates the cache only on a read miss, so only requested data is cached but it can be stale.

stem: Order events must be processed in strict sequence per customer, and duplicates are unacceptable. Which service configuration should be used?
options: An SQS standard queue with idempotent consumers
An SQS FIFO queue using the customer ID as the message group ID
An SNS standard topic with multiple subscribers
An SQS standard queue with a visibility timeout of 12 hours
explanation: FIFO queues guarantee ordering within a message group and exactly-once processing through deduplication. Using the customer ID as the group ID preserves per-customer order while still allowing parallelism across customers.
distractors: Standard queues are best-effort ordering, so strict sequence cannot be guaranteed even with idempotency.
SNS standard topics provide no ordering guarantee.
A long visibility timeout reduces duplicate delivery but does not provide ordering or deduplication.

stem: Fifty teams each need different access to different prefixes in one very large S3 bucket, and the bucket policy has become unmanageable. What should be used?
options: Separate buckets for every team
S3 Access Points, one per team, each with its own access policy
One IAM role per team with inline policies referencing the bucket
S3 Object Lambda Access Points
explanation: Access Points give each application or team its own named endpoint with a dedicated policy, which decomposes a single enormous bucket policy into manageable pieces without moving data.
distractors: Splitting the data into fifty buckets is a major migration and loses the shared data set.
IAM roles are still needed, but the problem stated is the bucket policy size and manageability, which Access Points solve directly.
Object Lambda Access Points transform data on retrieval; that is a different purpose.

stem: A question describes a workload that must survive the loss of an Availability Zone with the LEAST cost. Which answer shape should you prefer?
options: Resources in one Availability Zone with frequent backups
Resources in two Regions with cross-Region replication
Resources in three Regions with active-active routing
Resources in two Availability Zones within one Region
explanation: The requirement names an Availability Zone, which is an in-Region failure domain. Multi-AZ meets it at the lowest cost; multi-Region designs meet a stricter requirement that was not asked for and cost significantly more.
distractors: A single AZ with backups does not survive the loss of that AZ without downtime.
Multi-Region exceeds the stated requirement and violates the least-cost qualifier.
Three-Region active-active is dramatically more expensive than the requirement demands.

stem: Two teams in separate AWS accounts run services that exchange latency-sensitive traffic and want to place them in the same physical Availability Zone in eu-west-1. Both teams currently launch into "eu-west-1a". Which approach guarantees they end up in the same physical zone?
options: Keep using the AZ name eu-west-1a in both accounts, since names map to the same facility Region-wide
Enable Resource Access Manager sharing of the subnets so both accounts see the same AZ letter
Launch both services into a cluster placement group with the same name
Compare the AZ ID (for example euw1-az2) in each account and launch into the subnet whose AZ maps to the same ID
explanation: AZ names are shuffled independently per account, so eu-west-1a in one account can be a different facility from eu-west-1a in another. The AZ ID is the stable identifier of the physical zone and is the same across accounts.
distractors: AZ letters are deliberately randomised per account to spread load, so identical names do not imply the same physical zone.
RAM shares subnets, which would work but is heavier than needed and still requires you to identify the zone; on its own, sharing does not make the letters mean the same thing.
Placement groups are account-scoped constructs; a name in one account has no relationship to a group in another, and a cluster group cannot span accounts anyway.

stem: A regulator requires a payments platform to keep operating during a complete outage of the AWS Region it runs in. The platform currently spans three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. What is the MINIMUM change that satisfies the requirement?
options: Add resources in a second AWS Region with data replication and DNS failover
Add a fourth Availability Zone in the same Region
Move the platform behind CloudFront so edge locations serve traffic during the outage
Enable cross-zone load balancing on the load balancer
explanation: A Region is the largest failure boundary; the only way to survive its loss is to have the workload and its data available in a second Region. AZ redundancy protects against zone failure, not Regional failure.
distractors: More AZs in the same Region still share the Regional failure boundary.
Edge locations cache and terminate connections; they do not run the workload and cannot serve dynamic payment traffic when the origin Region is down.
Cross-zone load balancing spreads traffic across AZs within one Region; it has no effect on a Regional outage.

stem: A company migrates a self-managed PostgreSQL database on EC2 to Amazon RDS. The operations team wants to know which recurring tasks they can stop doing. Under the shared responsibility model, which task is now handled by AWS?
options: Rotating the database master password
Deciding which subnets and security groups the database is placed in
Applying operating-system and database-engine patches to the DB instance
Setting the backup retention period
explanation: RDS is a managed service: AWS owns the underlying host, OS and engine patching. Configuration choices such as network placement, credentials, backup retention and encryption remain the customer's responsibility.
distractors: Credentials are always yours; AWS never rotates your database passwords (Secrets Manager can automate it, but that is you configuring it).
Network placement is a customer configuration decision on any service that lives in a VPC.
Backup retention is a customer-set parameter; AWS runs the backups, you decide how long to keep them.

stem: An auditor reviewing a workload running on EC2 instances in a VPC asks the company to list the security controls that are its own responsibility rather than AWS's. Which items should be on that list? (Choose TWO.)
options: Physical access controls at the data centre hosting the instances
Patching the guest operating system on the instances
Security of the hypervisor isolating tenants on the host
Inbound and outbound rules in the instances' security groups
Replacement of failed disks in the underlying storage hardware
explanation: For IaaS services like EC2, AWS secures the facilities, hardware, hypervisor and network fabric; the customer owns everything from the guest OS upward, including OS patching, firewall rules (security groups and NACLs), application code and IAM.
distractors: Physical security of facilities is always AWS's responsibility ("security of the cloud").
The hypervisor is part of the infrastructure AWS operates and secures.
Hardware maintenance, including storage media, is handled by AWS.

stem: A build system stores intermediate artefacts in S3. Any artefact can be regenerated from source in about an hour, artefacts are read infrequently, and the finance team wants storage cost minimised. Which storage class is the MOST cost-effective while still appropriate?
options: S3 Standard
S3 Standard-IA
S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
explanation: One Zone-IA keeps the same eleven-nines durability but only within a single AZ, at roughly 20 percent less than Standard-IA. Losing the AZ loses the data, which is acceptable precisely because the artefacts are reproducible.
distractors: Standard is the most expensive class for infrequently read data and its multi-AZ resilience is not needed for reproducible artefacts.
Standard-IA is replicated across at least three AZs; the extra availability costs more than One Zone-IA and buys nothing for data you can regenerate.
Deep Archive has retrieval times of hours and minimum storage durations, so it does not suit artefacts that a build pipeline still needs to read.

stem: A compliance report states that a document archive on S3 Standard "will not become unreachable more than roughly an hour a year because AWS guarantees 99.999999999%". A solutions architect is asked to correct the statement. Which correction is accurate?
options: The figure is correct; eleven nines is the S3 Standard availability SLA
The figure applies only when versioning is enabled on the bucket
Eleven nines applies only to objects replicated across two Regions
Eleven nines is S3's durability figure (the data will not be lost); S3 Standard is designed for 99.99% availability
explanation: Durability answers "will the data still exist"; availability answers "can I reach it now". S3's eleven nines is durability, achieved by replicating objects across three or more AZs. S3 Standard targets 99.99% availability.
distractors: Availability and durability are different figures; conflating them is exactly the error in the report.
Versioning protects against accidental deletes and overwrites; it does not change the durability design figure.
Eleven-nines durability is achieved within a single Region by replicating across at least three AZs; cross-Region replication is not required.

stem: A team has a hardened, encrypted golden AMI in us-east-1 and must be able to launch identical instances in eu-central-1 for disaster recovery. When they try to launch from the AMI in eu-central-1 it does not appear in the list. What should they do?
options: Share the AMI with the eu-central-1 Region from the AMI permissions page
Enable AMI replication in the EC2 settings for the account
Copy the AMI to eu-central-1, encrypting the copy with a KMS key in that Region
Create the DR instances in us-east-1 and migrate them with the Application Migration Service
explanation: AMIs are Regional resources; to use one elsewhere you copy it to the target Region. Because the AMI is encrypted, the copy needs a KMS key that lives in the destination Region.
distractors: AMI sharing grants other accounts or an Organization launch permission; it does not move the image across Regions.
There is no account-level automatic AMI replication setting; cross-Region copies are explicit (though EC2 Image Builder can distribute them as part of a pipeline).
Application Migration Service is for lifting servers into AWS; it is far heavier than a cross-Region AMI copy and does not solve the underlying scope problem.

stem: A company that runs entirely in ap-southeast-2 is standing up a second deployment in eu-west-1. Which of its existing resources will have to be created again in eu-west-1 rather than reused as-is? (Choose TWO.)
options: The IAM roles used by the application
The VPC and its subnets
The Route 53 public hosted zone for the company domain
The Lambda functions that process uploads
The CloudFront distribution in front of the site
explanation: VPCs and Lambda functions are Regional, so a second Region needs its own copies. IAM, Route 53 and CloudFront are global services and are usable from every Region without duplication.
distractors: IAM is a global service; roles and policies apply in every Region.
Route 53 is global; a single hosted zone can route to endpoints in any Region.
CloudFront is global; one distribution can have origins in several Regions.

stem: A media company hosts images and video in a single Region. Users in South America and Asia complain of slow downloads. The company wants to improve latency for these users with the LEAST operational effort and cost.
options: Deploy full copies of the application in a Region on each continent
Increase the instance sizes serving the content
Move the content to S3 One Zone-IA in each Region for faster access
Put CloudFront in front of the content so it is cached at edge locations near the users
explanation: Edge locations exist to shorten the distance between users and the workload. CloudFront caches static content at 600+ points of presence, cutting latency without deploying the application anywhere new.
distractors: Extra Regions do reduce latency but mean running and synchronising multiple deployments, which is far more effort and cost than caching at the edge.
Larger instances address compute capacity, not geographic distance, which is the source of the latency.
One Zone-IA is a cost tier for infrequently accessed data; it does not move data closer to users and requires copying the content per Region.

stem: A design review of a three-tier web application shows the Application Load Balancer, the EC2 application instances and the RDS database all placed in public subnets across two Availability Zones. Which change makes the design MOST secure without affecting how users reach it?
options: Move the ALB, application instances and database into private subnets
Keep the ALB in the public subnets and move the application instances and the database into private subnets
Move only the database into a private subnet and protect the instances with a NACL
Replace the ALB with a NAT Gateway in the public subnets
explanation: In the baseline pattern only internet-facing components (the ALB, and a NAT Gateway if needed) live in public subnets. Compute and databases sit in private subnets and are reached only through the load balancer.
distractors: An internet-facing ALB must be in public subnets to receive user traffic; moving it private would break access.
Leaving application instances in public subnets keeps them directly reachable; a NACL reduces exposure but the baseline is that compute is private.
A NAT Gateway provides outbound internet for private subnets; it does not accept inbound user traffic and cannot replace a load balancer.

stem: An application runs in private subnets across two Availability Zones and reaches the internet through a single NAT Gateway in AZ-a. During a test that simulates the loss of AZ-a, instances in AZ-b lose internet access even though they are healthy. Why, and what is the fix?
options: NAT Gateways are Regional and the test disabled the Regional endpoint; retry the test
The security group on the AZ-b instances blocks outbound traffic during failover; add an outbound rule
A NAT Gateway is a zonal resource; deploy a NAT Gateway in each AZ and route each private subnet to the one in its own AZ
The Internet Gateway is attached to AZ-a; attach a second Internet Gateway for AZ-b
explanation: A NAT Gateway lives in one AZ, so a route table sending AZ-b traffic to a NAT Gateway in AZ-a fails when AZ-a fails. The resilient pattern is one NAT Gateway per AZ with per-AZ route tables.
distractors: NAT Gateways are zonal, not Regional; that is precisely the problem.
Security groups are unaffected by an AZ failure and the instances were working before the test.
An Internet Gateway is a Regional VPC attachment with no AZ affinity, and a VPC has exactly one.

stem: A web application on an Auto Scaling group writes user-uploaded files to the local disk of whichever instance handles the request. When instances are replaced during scale-in, files disappear. Which change aligns the design with the principle that instances should be disposable?
options: Enable termination protection on every instance in the group
Set the Auto Scaling group's minimum size equal to its maximum so instances are never terminated
Snapshot each instance's EBS volume before scale-in using a lifecycle hook
Store uploaded files in Amazon S3 and keep the instances stateless
explanation: In the baseline architecture state is pushed sideways to S3, DynamoDB or ElastiCache so any instance can be replaced at any moment. Uploaded objects belong in S3, not on instance disks.
distractors: Termination protection fights the Auto Scaling group and does not help when an instance fails outright.
Freezing the group size removes elasticity and still loses data when an instance fails or is replaced as unhealthy.
Snapshots preserve data but leave it inaccessible to the other instances; the application still cannot serve the files consistently.

stem: A company has 150 developers who all need the same set of permissions, and permissions change every few weeks. Today each developer's IAM user has policies attached individually. What is the approach with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an IAM group, attach the policies to the group, and add the developers to it
Create one shared IAM user for all developers and distribute its access keys
Attach an inline policy to each user with a script whenever permissions change
Create an IAM role for developers and nest the existing users inside it
explanation: Groups exist to organise human permissions: attach the policy once to the group and every member inherits it, so a change is one edit rather than 150.
distractors: Shared credentials destroy accountability and cannot be rotated without disrupting everyone.
Scripting inline policies works but scales badly and reinvents what groups do natively.
Users cannot be placed inside roles; roles are assumed, they do not contain members.

stem: A security engineer writes an S3 bucket policy and sets the Principal to the ARN of the "Analysts" IAM group so all analysts can read the bucket. The policy is rejected as invalid. What is the reason?
options: IAM groups cannot be used as a principal; the policy must name users or roles (or grant via an identity policy on the group)
Bucket policies only accept account IDs, not ARNs, in the Principal element
The group must be in a different account for a bucket policy to reference it
The bucket policy needs the Principal to be a service, not an identity
explanation: A group is only a container for attaching policies to users; it is not an identity that can make requests, so it cannot appear as a Principal in a resource-based policy. Attach an identity policy to the group instead, or name roles/users.
distractors: Bucket policies accept user, role and account ARNs as principals; the problem is the group specifically.
Same-account principals are perfectly valid in a bucket policy; the account boundary is not the issue.
Bucket policies routinely name IAM users, roles and accounts; services are only one kind of principal.

stem: A central logging bucket must accept PutObject from any account in the company's AWS Organization, including accounts created in the future, and from no one else. Which bucket policy design requires the LEAST maintenance?
options: List every current account ID in the Principal element and update it when accounts are added
Allow Principal "*" with a Condition on aws:PrincipalOrgID matching the Organization ID
Allow Principal "*" with a Condition on aws:SourceIp covering the corporate address ranges
Make the bucket public and rely on Block Public Access to filter external writers
explanation: The aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key matches any principal from any account in the named Organization, so new accounts are covered automatically and outsiders are excluded.
distractors: An explicit account list works today but has to be edited every time an account is created, which is the maintenance the question wants to avoid.
Source IP filtering does not identify AWS accounts; workloads inside AWS do not come from corporate IP ranges and outsiders could share an IP range.
Block Public Access blocks public policies; it does not selectively admit Organization members, and this design does not restrict to the Organization at all.

stem: A regulated company must ensure that no client can read or write objects in a bucket over unencrypted HTTP, regardless of which IAM identity they use. Which control enforces this?
options: Enable default encryption with SSE-S3 on the bucket
Attach a bucket policy that denies all s3 actions when aws:SecureTransport is false
Enable S3 Block Public Access on the bucket
Require the s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption header on uploads
explanation: aws:SecureTransport is true only for HTTPS requests. A Deny statement with a Bool condition on it being false rejects every plaintext request, and being an explicit Deny it overrides any Allow from any identity policy.
distractors: Default encryption protects data at rest; it says nothing about how requests travel over the network.
Block Public Access controls anonymous and public access, not the transport protocol.
That header condition forces objects to be encrypted server-side on upload; it does not require TLS on the connection.

stem: Administrators may delete objects from a critical bucket, but only when they have authenticated with a hardware MFA device in their current session. Which policy element implements this?
options: A Condition using aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent on the s3:DeleteObject statement
A Condition using aws:SecureTransport on the s3:DeleteObject statement
A permissions boundary on the administrators' roles that excludes s3:DeleteObject
Enabling versioning on the bucket so deletes can be undone
explanation: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is set on requests made with credentials obtained after MFA. Requiring it (or denying when it is false) on the delete action ties the sensitive operation to an MFA-authenticated session.
distractors: aws:SecureTransport checks for HTTPS, not for multi-factor authentication.
A boundary caps maximum permissions; it cannot make an action conditional on how the caller authenticated.
Versioning mitigates the damage of a delete but does not restrict who or how the delete is performed.

stem: An application running under an IAM role in Account A must send messages to an SQS queue owned by Account B. The team wants to avoid creating any new roles or performing role assumption. What is required?
options: Nothing beyond the role's identity policy; SQS trusts all accounts in the same Region
A queue policy in Account B alone is sufficient; the role's identity policy is not consulted for cross-account requests
A queue policy in Account B that allows sqs:SendMessage for the Account A role, plus an identity policy on the role allowing the action
Create an IAM user in Account B and embed its access keys in the application
explanation: Resource-based policies such as SQS queue policies carry a Principal and can grant another account directly without role assumption. Cross-account, though, both sides must agree: the queue policy names the caller and the caller's own identity policy must allow the action.
distractors: There is no implicit cross-account trust; without a resource policy naming the caller, the request is denied.
A resource policy alone is enough only within a single account; across accounts the caller's identity policy must also allow the action.
Access keys in application code are the pattern the exam always marks wrong; the resource policy path needs no long-lived credentials.

stem: An IAM user in Account X has no identity-based policies attached and belongs to no groups. A bucket policy on a bucket in the same Account X explicitly allows that user s3:GetObject on all objects. There are no SCPs or permissions boundaries. What happens when the user downloads an object?
options: Denied, because a principal with no identity policy has no permissions at all
Denied, because bucket policies can only grant access to principals in other accounts
Allowed, because within one account a resource-based policy Allow is sufficient on its own
Allowed only if the user first assumes a role that trusts the bucket
explanation: In the evaluation order, once no explicit Deny and no SCP block the request, an Allow in a resource-based policy is enough for a same-account principal. The identity policy is only required to agree for cross-account access.
distractors: The implicit deny applies only when nothing allows the request; here the bucket policy does.
Bucket policies name principals in the same account routinely; that is how same-account resource-based grants work.
No role assumption is needed; the user is named directly and buckets do not "trust" roles.

stem: An IAM user belongs to a group whose policy allows dynamodb:* on all tables. A policy attached directly to the user contains a Deny for dynamodb:DeleteTable. The user attempts to delete a table. What is the outcome, and why?
options: Allowed, because group policies are evaluated after user policies and override them
Allowed, because the wildcard Allow is more specific than the single-action Deny
Denied, because the group policy applies only to console actions
Denied, because an explicit Deny anywhere in the applicable policies overrides every Allow
explanation: Policy evaluation checks for an explicit Deny first; if any applicable policy denies the action, the request is denied and no Allow can override it, regardless of where the Allow is attached.
distractors: There is no precedence between group and user policies; all applicable statements are evaluated together and Deny wins.
Specificity is not a factor in IAM evaluation; explicit Deny always takes precedence.
Group policies apply to every API call, whether from the console, CLI or SDK.

stem: A company attaches an SCP to the root of its Organization that denies all actions outside eu-west-1 and eu-central-1. An engineer notices that an administrator in the Organization's management account can still launch instances in us-east-1. What explains this?
options: SCPs take up to 24 hours to propagate to the management account
SCPs do not apply to the management account; only member accounts are restricted
The AdministratorAccess policy in the management account overrides SCPs
SCPs attached to the root are advisory and must be attached to each OU to be enforced
explanation: Service control policies filter permissions for member accounts, including their root users, but they never restrict the management account. Sensitive work should therefore not run in the management account.
distractors: SCP changes take effect promptly; propagation delay is not the explanation.
No IAM policy in a member account can override an SCP; the management account is exempt because SCPs simply do not apply there, not because a policy wins.
SCPs attached to the root are inherited by every OU and account beneath it and are fully enforced on member accounts.

stem: A team created an IAM role with a permissions policy allowing full access to a DynamoDB table and assigned it as a Lambda function's execution role. The function fails to start with an error saying the role cannot be assumed. What must be changed?
options: Add dynamodb:* to the role's permissions policy for the Lambda service
Attach the role to the Lambda function's VPC configuration
Add lambda.amazonaws.com as a Principal in the role's trust policy
Grant the function's IAM user sts:AssumeRole on the role
explanation: A role has two policies: the trust policy decides who may assume it, and the permissions policy decides what it can do once assumed. Lambda assumes the execution role, so the trust policy must name the Lambda service principal.
distractors: The permissions policy governs what the role can do; the error is about who is allowed to assume it, which is the trust policy.
VPC configuration controls networking and has nothing to do with role assumption.
Lambda functions do not run as IAM users; the service itself assumes the role via the trust policy.

stem: A mobile app lets users sign in with Google or Apple and then upload photos directly to an S3 bucket, each user only to their own prefix. The app must not contain long-lived AWS credentials. Which design is recommended?
options: Use Cognito Identity Pools to exchange the social login token for temporary AWS credentials scoped to the user
Have the app call sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML with the Google token
Use IAM Identity Center to federate the users and assign a permission set
Store an IAM user's access keys in the app and restrict the keys with a bucket policy
explanation: For app users authenticating with web identity providers, Cognito Identity Pools is the recommended wrapper around AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity: it vends short-lived credentials for a role whose policy can be scoped per user identity.
distractors: Google and Apple sign-in are OIDC/web identity providers, not SAML; the matching API is AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, ideally through Cognito.
Identity Center is for workforce access to AWS accounts, not for consumer users of a mobile application.
Access keys shipped in a client app can be extracted and are long-lived; a bucket policy cannot compensate for that.

stem: A policy requires that IAM users only perform destructive CLI operations with credentials backed by MFA. An operator has an IAM user with MFA enabled but the CLI uses long-lived access keys. Which STS call obtains MFA-backed temporary credentials for the same user?
options: sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
sts:GetFederationToken
sts:GetSessionToken with the MFA device serial and code
sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML
explanation: GetSessionToken returns temporary credentials for the calling IAM user; when called with an MFA device and code, the resulting session carries aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent = true and satisfies MFA-conditioned policies.
distractors: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity exchanges an OIDC token from an identity provider for role credentials; it is not for IAM users with MFA.
GetFederationToken issues credentials for a federated user via a proxy application and is not the MFA-elevation mechanism for an IAM user.
AssumeRoleWithSAML is for corporate SAML federation, not for an existing IAM user's own session.

stem: An external audit firm that operates from its own AWS account needs read-only access to a company's account for six weeks. Which approach is MOST secure and requires the least ongoing management?
options: Create an IAM user for the auditors with ReadOnlyAccess and email them the access keys
Share the root user's credentials with the audit firm for the duration
Add the auditors' account to the company's Organization
Create a role with ReadOnlyAccess whose trust policy allows the audit firm's account and requires an sts:ExternalId
explanation: Cross-account access is done with a role: the trust policy names the third party's account, they assume it for temporary credentials, and the ExternalId prevents the confused deputy problem. Removing access at the end is deleting one role.
distractors: Long-lived access keys sent by email are exactly the anti-pattern roles exist to avoid.
The root user must never be shared; it cannot be restricted by IAM policies.
Joining an Organization is a governance relationship, not an access mechanism, and gives the auditors far more than they need.

stem: A newly created AWS account will be handed to a product team. Before it is used, a security review requires the root user to be locked down. Which actions should be taken? (Choose TWO.)
options: Enable multi-factor authentication on the root user
Attach a permissions boundary to the root user restricting it to billing
Delete any access keys belonging to the root user and use IAM identities for day-to-day work
Move the root user into an IAM group with limited permissions
Rotate the root access keys every 90 days and store them in Secrets Manager
explanation: The root user cannot be restricted by IAM policies, so the defence is to protect it (MFA) and remove standing credentials (no access keys), using it only for the handful of tasks that require it.
distractors: IAM policies, including permissions boundaries, do not apply to the root user.
The root user is not an IAM user and cannot be placed in a group.
Root access keys should not exist at all; rotating them keeps an unnecessary long-lived credential alive.

stem: An engineer accidentally applied a bucket policy that denies all principals every S3 action on the bucket, and now no IAM administrator can view or delete the policy. How can access be restored?
options: Sign in as the account root user and delete the bucket policy
Attach AdministratorAccess to a new IAM user and delete the policy
Open an AWS Support case; only AWS can remove a bucket policy
Wait for the policy to expire; deny statements are temporary
explanation: An explicit Deny for all principals in the bucket policy blocks every IAM identity. Removing an unusable bucket policy is one of the specific tasks reserved for the account root user.
distractors: The explicit Deny in the bucket policy applies to every IAM principal, including a brand-new administrator.
The root user can fix this without AWS Support involvement.
Policies do not expire; the deny stays until it is removed.

stem: A security team wants a continuous list of every S3 bucket, IAM role, KMS key and SQS queue that is accessible from outside their AWS Organization, and to be told when a new one appears. Which service should they enable?
options: IAM credential report
IAM Access Analyzer
IAM Access Advisor
AWS Trusted Advisor
explanation: IAM Access Analyzer evaluates resource-based policies and reports resources shared with principals outside the account or Organization, generating findings as new external access is granted.
distractors: The credential report is an account-wide CSV about IAM users' passwords and keys, not about resource sharing.
Access Advisor shows which services an identity has actually used, to help trim its permissions; it does not analyse resource policies.
Trusted Advisor has a few S3 permission checks, but it is not a continuous analysis of resource policies across services and Organization boundaries.

stem: A team needs about twenty small development servers that sit almost idle most of the day, with occasional short bursts when tests run. Which instance family is the MOST cost-effective fit?
options: c family (compute optimised)
r family (memory optimised)
t family (burstable general purpose)
i family (storage optimised)
explanation: Burstable t instances earn CPU credits while idle and spend them during bursts, so a low, spiky baseline is exactly their design point at the lowest hourly price.
distractors: Compute-optimised instances suit sustained CPU-heavy work like batch and encoding; they are oversized and pricier for idle dev boxes.
Memory-optimised instances target caches and large databases, not idle development servers.
Storage-optimised instances come with local NVMe for very high IOPS; nothing here needs that.

stem: A company runs a fleet of m5.large instances 24/7 for a mature application and is certain the instance type and Region will not change for the next three years. It wants the LARGEST possible discount.
options: Three-year Standard Reserved Instances for m5.large in that Region
Three-year Compute Savings Plan
Three-year Convertible Reserved Instances
Spot Instances with a mixed instances policy
explanation: Standard RIs give the deepest discount when the configuration is fixed, and can be resold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace if plans change. The question stresses an unchanging type, which is the RI cue.
distractors: A Compute Savings Plan buys flexibility across families, Regions and Fargate/Lambda at a somewhat smaller discount; flexibility is not needed here.
Convertible RIs allow exchanging for another family at the cost of a smaller discount; the workload does not need that.
Spot can be interrupted with two minutes' notice and is unsuitable for a fleet that must run continuously.

stem: A financial application must always be able to launch a fixed number of a specific instance type in a specific Availability Zone, even during Regional capacity shortages, and the company also wants a discount for the steady usage. Which option provides BOTH?
options: Compute Savings Plan
EC2 Instance Savings Plan
Zonal Reserved Instances in that Availability Zone
Regional Reserved Instances
explanation: A zonal RI reserves capacity in the named AZ as well as providing the billing discount. Savings Plans and Regional RIs are billing constructs only and do not reserve capacity.
distractors: Savings Plans are purely a pricing commitment; they never reserve capacity.
An EC2 Instance Savings Plan locks a family and Region for a discount but still provides no capacity reservation.
Regional RIs float across AZs for the discount but do not reserve capacity in a specific AZ.

stem: A rendering farm on Spot Instances loses large numbers of nodes at once and jobs stall. The team wants to keep the Spot discount while reducing how often work is interrupted. Which changes help MOST? (Choose TWO.)
options: Request capacity across many instance types and Availability Zones using EC2 Fleet or Spot Fleet
Use the capacity-optimized allocation strategy instead of lowest-price
Request a Spot block for a guaranteed six-hour uninterrupted window
Move all nodes to a single instance type in a cluster placement group
Set the Spot maximum price to ten times the On-Demand price
explanation: Spot is made reliable by diversity: spreading requests across many pools means one pool being reclaimed does not empty the fleet, and capacity-optimized picks the pools with the most spare capacity, which are least likely to be interrupted.
distractors: Spot blocks (defined-duration Spot) are no longer available; a guaranteed uninterrupted window is not something Spot offers.
Concentrating on one type in one placement group is the opposite of diversification and increases the chance everything is reclaimed together.
Interruptions happen when AWS needs the capacity back, not because of your price; overpaying does not prevent reclamation.

stem: A company runs five instances that each host a critical, non-replicated component. A single hardware failure must never take down more than one of them, and they may be spread across Availability Zones. Which placement group type is appropriate?
options: Cluster placement group
No placement group; instead put all five in one dedicated host
Partition placement group
Spread placement group
explanation: A spread placement group places each instance on distinct underlying hardware and can span AZs, giving maximum isolation for a small number of critical instances (up to seven per AZ).
distractors: Cluster packs instances into one rack for low latency, which is exactly the shared failure domain the requirement forbids.
A single dedicated host is one physical server, so a hardware failure would take down all five.
Partition groups separate groups of instances onto different racks; they suit large rack-aware distributed systems rather than isolating individual instances.

stem: An analytics application takes 20 minutes to load a large in-memory dataset after every boot. It is used only during business hours and the team wants to stop paying for compute overnight without the long warm-up each morning. What should they do?
options: Stop the instance each evening and start it each morning
Terminate the instance each evening and launch from an AMI each morning
Hibernate the instance each evening so RAM is preserved to the encrypted root volume and restored on start
Leave the instance running and downsize it overnight
explanation: Hibernate writes RAM contents to the encrypted EBS root volume and restores them on start, so the application resumes with its dataset in memory while compute charges stop; the root volume must be encrypted and large enough to hold RAM.
distractors: A stopped instance loses its RAM, so the 20-minute load happens again every morning.
Terminating loses both RAM and the root volume by default; the warm-up would repeat.
Resizing requires a stop, which loses RAM, and continuing to run overnight still incurs compute cost.

stem: An operations team must apply the same configuration command to 500 EC2 instances across several Auto Scaling groups without opening SSH and without logging in to each instance. What should they use?
options: EC2 Instance Connect with a script looping over instance IDs
AWS Systems Manager Run Command targeting the instances by tag
A bastion host with a shared key pair
User data, by rebooting every instance
explanation: SSM Run Command executes a command across a fleet selected by tags or resource groups through the SSM agent, with no inbound ports and no per-instance sessions.
distractors: Instance Connect pushes ephemeral SSH keys to individual public instances; it still requires port 22 and one connection per instance.
A bastion reintroduces open SSH and shared long-lived keys, the pattern modern answers avoid.
User data runs only at first boot, not on reboot, and rebooting a fleet to run one command is disruptive.

stem: A regulatory requirement states that a company's instances must not share physical hardware with other AWS customers. There is no bring-your-own-licence requirement and no need to see or control physical sockets. Which option satisfies the requirement at the LOWEST cost?
options: Dedicated Hosts
Dedicated Instances
Instances in a cluster placement group
On-Demand instances with enhanced networking
explanation: Dedicated Instances run on single-tenant hardware but AWS controls placement and you get no socket visibility, which is all this requirement needs. Dedicated Hosts add physical-server visibility and placement control at higher cost, which only socket-bound licensing justifies.
distractors: Dedicated Hosts also isolate hardware but reserve an entire physical server; they cost more and their extra visibility is only needed for per-socket/per-core licences.
Placement groups control proximity for latency; they say nothing about tenancy.
Default tenancy shares hosts with other customers, whatever the networking option.

stem: A company must route all inbound and outbound traffic for several VPCs through a fleet of third-party next-generation firewall appliances, transparently and at scale, without changing application code. Which load balancer should front the appliances?
options: Application Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer
explanation: Gateway Load Balancer operates at layer 3 with GENEVE encapsulation, steering traffic transparently through third-party virtual appliances and scaling them like any other target group.
distractors: An ALB terminates HTTP and routes on content; it cannot pass raw IP packets through inspection appliances.
An NLB balances TCP/UDP connections to targets; it does not transparently insert appliances into the packet path.
The Classic Load Balancer is legacy layer 4/7 balancing and has no appliance-insertion capability.
